idea:credit-proof.reply:
The research is done: eleven setups compared, every price read on the vendor's own page today. Full report on the hub at /__hub/plan?card=make-sure-a-busy-launch-month-cannot-pau, and in docs/HU-HOSTING-OPTIONS-2026-10-11.md.

For the launch month: stay on Netlify. Turn on auto-recharge (500 credits for $5 each time they run out; off by default, only you can turn it on) and delete the duplicate project. Moving hosts three weeks before a launch is the bigger risk. One catch: Netlify has no spending ceiling, so the choice there is a pause or an open-ended bill. A 10,000-visitor day works out to about 252 credits, so the plan holds about 34,000 visitors a month before buying more.

For the next year: move to Cloudflare. Its static pages are free and unlimited (confirmed again on Cloudflare's own page: "Requests to static assets are free and unlimited"), so a launch day, a viral week or a bot flood costs $0, or $5 a month on the paid plan. It is about a day of work: netlify.toml stays the source and a build step writes Cloudflare's files from it, the signup form and the per diem lookup each become a small route at the same address, and the version stamp gets one more line. Your hands: a Cloudflare account and moving the domain's DNS off Namecheap, which also means setting up Cloudflare's email routing first, because Namecheap's free forwarding stops when the DNS moves.

If the site really grows: Cloudflare still costs $0 to $5 for the static site. Second choice is Amazon CloudFront's flat-rate plans ($15 or $200 a month), which never bill for overage.

Not worth it here: GitHub Pages (no security headers at all, no redirects), Firebase's free plan (the site is switched off when it runs out), Vercel's free plan (fine with a Ko-fi link, but it stops the site for 30 days past about 38,000 visitors a month).

Two things the research corrected: the built site is 62 MB now, not 40, and the Cost of Living tool uses a Netlify Function (the per diem lookup) that any move has to carry.

idea:linkedin-newsletter.reply: Yes, it is easy. LinkedIn's help page (checked tonight) says any member can create one: Write article from the share box, then the Manage menu, then Create newsletter, then a name and a description. The option only shows if your account has newsletter access, and the page does not say how that is granted, so look for it first. When you create it you can invite all your connections and followers; anyone who follows you later is invited automatically, and every edition notifies subscribers by email. Setup is about half an hour; keeping it going is about two hours a week. Check the employer social media policy first (Start here, number 3).

idea:public-repo-decision.note:
I thought the repo was private? should we still be hosting our entire website on github?

How can you fix this?
idea:public-repo-decision.reply: It is public. GitHub answers for dmeitel/Healthcare_Uncharted_Site_v2 without a login (checked tonight): public since April 1, 0 stars, 0 forks. GitHub does not host the website; Netlify does. GitHub only stores the code and its history, and Netlify builds the site from it. So making the repo private changes who can read the code and the notes, not how the site runs, and Netlify builds from private repos too. Two things to know: anything public since April may already have been copied, so private hides it from now on but cannot take the past back; and on a private repo GitHub's free plan gives 2,000 Actions minutes a month (the daily tests and the relay keep-awake use some of that). Recommendation: make it private before the launch (Settings, General, Danger zone, Change visibility), and scrub the medical details out of DECISIONS.md either way. Whether to host somewhere other than Netlify is the research running on the Netlify card.

idea:rt-in-nursing-homes.reply: Yes, they overlap, and that is the right way to build them. The map ideas sort into the two maps the site already has. State numbers go on the Population Health Map as new layers: the RT pipeline gap, home respiratory care, the share of nursing homes reporting any RT hours, the workforce outlook. Places go on the Hospital Operations Map as new facility layers: nursing homes with their RT hours, long-term care hospitals, quality on the hospital cards, shortage areas. So it is one data milestone instead of six separate tools, and "where vent patients go after the ICU" becomes a story that walks across those layers.
